Industrial food recipe replacement for sustainability? Does the capacity of a neural ingredient-substitution ranker improve its ranking of sustainable replacements, measured as Hit@1 on Recipe1MSubs — once the 20.56 versus 34.53 baseline gap between Meta's GISMo and Rita et al.'s GISMo reimplementation is explained? First reproduce both numbers in one harness: Meta's official GISMo code against the Rita et al. protocol, isolating the difference (data split, candidate set, preprocessing). Then run the width sweep 64–512 only inside whichever protocol reproduces, and report the width trend under both.", "root_link":"is the root question, tested on the same ranker-capacity lever but only after the cross-protocol baseline is reconciled","compute_open":"the sweep budget stays as before; the new cost is a one-off reproduction of both baselines, roughly a few machine-hours, before the 4-width by 5-seed sweep","sequential":"yes: baseline reconciliation must finish before the width sweep means anything","changes":"Adds a prerequisite reconciliation stage and judges the result against both named programmes' published numbers instead of Meta's alone. Closes the 'unresolved discrepancy' gap and makes the width conclusion transferable between the Meta GISMo and Imperial Hyperfoods programmes."},{"id":"V2","title":"Capacity sweep judged on industrial-formulation proxies rather than home-recipe Hit@1","text":"Industrial food ingredient replacement for sustainability? Industrial food recipe replacement for sustainability? Does increasing substitution-ranker capacity buy better ranking on formulation-relevant targets rather than only on home recipes? Keep GISMo's Recipe1MSubs ranker and protocol, but judge the width sweep 64–512 against quantities tied to formulation: retrieval of substitutes that match declared functional role (e.g. emulsifier, binder, sweetener) and, where the data allow, an ingredient-level environmental proxy such as category-level footprint ranking. Report whether the width trend on those targets matches the Hit@1 trend.", "root_link":"is the root question, aimed at the industrial formulation half rather than the home-recipe half","compute_open":"unchanged; the added work is labelling or mapping substitutes to functional roles and footprint categories, not extra training compute","sequential":"no: the functional-role and footprint labels can be built in parallel with the width sweep","changes":"Changes the quantity more compute is judged on, from Hit@1 on home recipes to formulation-relevant ranking quality. Answers the gap that no programme links this metric to industrial formulation or environmental footprint."},{"id":"V3","title":"Does capacity buy anything over the fine-tuned LLM substitution baselines?","text":"Industrial food ingredient replacement for sustainability? Industrial food recipe replacement for sustainability? Does ranker capacity buy better sustainable-substitute ranking than the LLM baselines already published in the same protocol? Reproduce Rita et al.'s Recipe1MSubs setup, including their GISMo baseline and fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and TinyLlama numbers (Hit@1 34.53 to 38.03), then sweep the GISMo ranker's ingredient-encoder width 64–512 with five seeds and compare each width against those fixed LLM baselines. The question is whether any width closes the gap to the fine-tuned LLMs, not whether width beats GISMo's own baseline.", "root_link":"is the root question, tested as a capacity-versus-LLM comparison in the programme that actually publishes on it","compute_open":"the sweep cost is as before; an added cost is matching Rita et al.'s fine-tuning protocol closely enough that their 34.53 and 38.03 numbers stand as fixed comparators","sequential":"partly: the LLM baselines are fixed published comparators, so the width sweep can start immediately","changes":"Changes the comparison it is judged against, from GISMo's 20.56 baseline to the Imperial Hyperfoods fine-tuned-LLM numbers.
